meta.title: Meteotsunamis
meta.speaker: NOAA Ocean Podcast
meta.blurb: A tsunami caused by weather instead of an earthquake — and it can happen on the Great Lakes.
meta.credit: NOAA Ocean Podcast, "Meteotsunamis" (Episode 70). U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, National Ocean Service. Public domain (work of the U.S. Government).

summary.text:
A meteotsunami is exactly what it sounds like: a tsunami driven by the weather. Instead of an earthquake or an undersea landslide, fast-moving storm systems disturb the air pressure and push up a wave that can reach several meters [1]. The waves behave like tsunami waves — minutes to two hours long, not the ten-second waves you see at the beach [2] — but carry far less energy, so they often hit just one harbor or one estuary [3].

NOAA scientist Greg Dusek's study found they are far more common than anyone expected: on the order of 25 a year along the U.S. east coast [4], though 90% are under about a foot and a half [5]. The Carolinas see the most, because that coast catches summertime thunderstorms, nor'easters and tropical storms alike [6].

The threshold to remember: events over about two feet are where impacts start — swimmers in summer, added flooding and erosion in storm season [7].

So 90% of the events we found were under about a foot and a half.
North Carolina is exposed to summertime thunderstorms, which can drive events, wintertime storms like nor'easters, which can drive events, and then tropical storms.
what we propose is that events over about two feet are where you start worrying about potential impacts.

chapters.title: How they differ from seismic tsunamis

at.quote: I think when a lot of people think about, hear the word tsunami, they immediately think to like the Japanese tsunami that occurred a number of years ago,
Even as early as 1954, there was a documented event of a meteo tsunami in the Great Lakes.
And what did you discover in your study?
Certain locations along the east coast tend to see events more than others,
But we're mostly worried about those events that cause waves over a couple of feet, right?

concepts.definition: A tsunami-length wave generated by air-pressure disturbances from fast-moving storm systems rather than by seismic activity — "meteorologically driven" is literal.

cite.quote: instead of tsunamis driven by an earthquake or an underwater landslide, they're driven by the weather and specifically, typically fast moving storm systems, which tend to cause a wave on the ocean surface.

concepts.definition: What separates tsunami-type waves from ordinary surf: duration. Beach waves last seconds; meteotsunamis are long rises and falls of the water level itself.

cite.quote: they're not like the waves you see at the beach, which might be 10 seconds long. These tend to be anywhere from a couple minutes to two hours long.

concepts.definition: The deadliest documented U.S. meteotsunami: a roughly ten-foot wave on Lake Michigan that killed seven people — proof the Great Lakes are exposed.

cite.quote: it was reportedly on the order of 10 feet high and actually ended up causing seven deaths near Chicago.
